correctness.rationale: Deleting the marked leaves leaves a bipartite tree, and the attachments to unmarked opposite-part vertices give exactly the all-marked-leaves probabilities in (1), including when the core is K_{1,1}. An entirely marked part is impossible by the sum of its degrees. Inclusion–exclusion gives independent baseline empty-box vectors and the Stirling laws. For the edge tilt put q=w−1. From the conditional incidences in (3)–(4), r_u−p=−(a−1)α_u/(ab), s_v−p=−(b−1)β_v/(ab), and h_uv−r_u−s_v+p=−α_uβ_v/(ab). The quadratic tilt coefficient ph_uv−r_us_v is the same as the linear coefficient, since p+(a−1)(b−1)/(ab)=1. This yields the stated q(1+q) factor; the denominator is positive even at deletion. Neither contrast vector vanishes, and each has zero sum, giving the signs, ranks and zero sums. Conditioning on both leaf counts preserves symmetry among edges under the uniform law; the number of selected edges remains fixed, so every edge still has inclusion probability p. The tilt consequently leaves the entire joint count law unchanged. This need not preserve independence of the labeled vectors.
residual_risks: The recorded finite enumeration is corroboration, not an all-parameter proof. The all-size algebra and conditioning were independently checked.

value.rationale: A single conductance is a natural minimal perturbation of a graph with independent cross-part leaf vectors. The full covariance matrix resolves where dependence appears, where it reverses sign, and where it disappears; simultaneously the aggregate observers cannot detect any tilt. The exact factor and ranks are useful precisely because invariance of total counts alone misses the local structure.
residual_risks: This is a one-edge cross-part result, not a classification of arbitrary conductance matrices or within-part leaf covariances.
